Lessons.Title: Points and Lines All Around
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: identify parallel and intersecting straight lines and draw them accurately in familiar places. The 2021 Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 4 source revisits these line relationships in quadrilateral drawings, a neighbourhood map and a classroom design task.

Warm-up (10 min), Which One Doesn't Belong: Four-sided Shapes: compare four original quadrilateral figures. Choose and explain a property such as a pair of parallel sides, equal directions or a square corner. More than one answer can be defensible, depending on the property explained. The teacher must inspect lawfully available original drawings; this screen does not assert their appearance.

Activity 1 (15 min), Spot Lines and Line Segments: inspect the 2021 original Staten Island neighbourhood map and label examples of distinct parallel segments, crossing segments and square corners where visibly evidenced. The original source cites a historical Sanborn map as public-domain material; this Edulytics lesson does not reproduce the map. A teacher checks visual identifications against the actual source.

Activity 2 (20 min), Draw and Design with Lines: sketch part of a classroom and include AT LEAST THREE pairs of parallel segments. Also include segments intersecting at right angles (square corners); label and justify the pairs. A drawn horizontal shelf edge and two vertical door jambs can help plan a design, but the teacher must verify the child's actual diagram meets all conditions.

First-party Cool-down (5 min, NOT publisher Word Fun): draw two different parallel line segments and a transversal crossing both. Mark the intersections, and explain why the two original segments remain parallel. The original publisher 2021 Cool-down is not reproduced or asserted to have been seen.

Digital Practice reuses the Grade 4 Unit 7 exact dot-grid relationship family for parallel versus intersecting complete lines, with independently encoded row and column positions. It is recognition support only; the actual quadrilateral artwork, map interpretation, classroom sketch, oral justification and measured right-angle drawings require teacher assessment. Infinite geometric lines and finite drawn segments are distinguished explicitly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel lines and segments
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two distinct coplanar complete lines stay the same direction and never meet. Two finite segments are parallel if their supporting complete lines are parallel.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check direction and distinct position, not whether the drawn strokes look close or far apart.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two vertical sides of a rectangular window are parallel line segments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intersecting lines and square corners
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two straight lines intersect if they meet. A square corner forms when the crossing segments meet at a right angle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A right-angle crossing is one type of intersection; not every intersection makes a right angle.
KeyConcepts.Example: A vertical door jamb meeting a horizontal top edge at a square corner gives a right-angle intersection.

KeyConcepts.Title: Transversal across parallel lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: A transversal is another line that crosses two or more lines at different locations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Drawing a transversal across two parallel lines does not change the fact that those two lines are parallel.
KeyConcepts.Example: One horizontal line crossing two different vertical parallel lines creates two intersection points.

WorkedExamples.Title: Parallel lines on a first-party dot grid
WorkedExamples.Question: h passes through row 1, columns 1 and 4. g passes through row 3, columns 1 and 4. Are these different extended lines parallel or intersecting?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the direction and positions of the supporting straight lines.
Steps: The two points for h lie on the same row; h is horizontal.
The two points for g lie on another row; g is also horizontal.
The complete lines have the same direction and different rows, so they cannot meet.
WorkedExamples.Check: Different row numbers prove they are distinct; the complete lines never share a point.

WorkedExamples.Title: A transversal crossing two parallels
WorkedExamples.Question: Two different vertical straight lines lie along column 1 and column 4 on a grid. A horizontal line along row 3 crosses both. Are the two vertical lines now intersecting each other?
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish the relationship of the two original vertical lines from their intersections with a third line.
Steps: The two vertical lines are both straight up-down and occupy different columns, so they are parallel.
The horizontal transversal crosses the first at row 3,col 1 and the second at row 3,col 4.
The two original vertical lines do not cross each other; a third intersecting line does not change this.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. The two vertical lines remain parallel; the transversal intersects each separately.
WorkedExamples.Check: Exactly two crossing points with the transversal, but none shared between the vertical parallels.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source activity — historical map (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: On the original 2021 neighbourhood map, identify and label pairs of straight parallel or intersecting street-edge segments; justify each identification.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the supplied legal map or a properly credited classroom source, trace visible straight segments and compare orientation and crossing.
Steps: Locate two segments you believe have supporting lines in the same direction.
For an intersecting pair, mark and explain the common point if the diagram supports it.
Teacher checks actual drawn map positions, captions and student explanations; do not invent map features.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Dependent on the original figure, teacher-scored.
WorkedExamples.Check: No copied Sanborn map image or verified digital picture-scoring is claimed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source activity — classroom design (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: Sketch part of a classroom containing at least THREE pairs of parallel segments and intersecting segments that make square corners.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw and annotate enough distinct straight segments to satisfy both geometric constraints.
Steps: List three candidate parallel pairs, for example vertical edges of two doors, horizontal edges of a shelf, and opposite edges of a window frame.
Draw each pair with matching direction. Label their endpoints or mark them clearly.
Find at least one horizontal-vertical crossing at a square corner; mark the right angle and explain it. Teacher checks the whole composition.
WorkedExamples.Answer: An original drawing with >=3 verifiable parallel segment pairs and at least one right-angle intersection.
WorkedExamples.Check: Correctness requires a real drawing and teacher review, not a numeric selection.

WorkedExamples.Title: Edulytics first-party Cool-down — transversal (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw two parallel straight segments and one transversal crossing both, label intersections, and justify.
WorkedExamples.Method: Start with two different vertical segments then add one horizontal segment crossing both.
Steps: Draw two vertical segments in different columns, of sufficient length to cross a horizontal stroke.
Draw the horizontal stroke so it meets each vertical segment; mark both intersections.
Explain that each vertical segment's complete line remains parallel to the other, despite the transversal.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Two distinct parallel segments plus a crossing transversal with two marked intersections.
WorkedExamples.Check: Independent first-party task, not the protected publisher 2021 Word Fun Cool-down.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming that crossing a third line means two originally parallel lines are no longer parallel.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each original line's direction and position remain unchanged; the transversal intersects both separately.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Classify the relationship of the specified pair, not of each with unrelated lines.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling any two crossing segments a square corner.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A square corner requires a right angle, not just an intersection.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the 90° angle of the actual drawn segments using the teacher's construction guidance.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating short, separate segments as necessarily parallel.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Finite segments may not touch even if their complete supporting lines would meet.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the directions of the complete straight lines, and distinguish non-touching from parallel.

SummaryPoints: Parallel pairs: supporting lines have the same direction and distinct positions; intersecting pairs share a crossing point.
A transversal can cross two parallel lines without changing their relationship.
Source teacher-only tasks: four-sided-shape talk, historical map identification, and original classroom drawing with >=3 parallel pairs plus square corners.
Supplementary digital dot-grid classification cannot certify the publisher's map artwork or the student's constructed drawing.
